explanation: Basal plates are the anterior (ventral) portions of the alar and basal plates in the developing neural tube. The basal plate gives rise to motor neurons that form the VENTRAL (anterior) horns of the spinal cord, which contain lower motor neurons. The alar plates form the dorsal (posterior) horns. Lateral horns appear only at T1-L2 levels (sympathetic neurons).
keyConcept: Basal plates form VENTRAL HORNS of spinal cord (motor neurons); alar plates form dorsal horns (sensory neurons).

explanation: The red nucleus is a motor relay center in the midbrain that develops from the NEUROEPITHELIUM of the midbrain, NOT from neural crest. Neural crest derivatives include spinal ganglia (sensory), arachnoid mater, suprarenal medulla (chromaffin cells), and sympathetic ganglia. This makes B the exception.
keyConcept: Red nucleus from midbrain neuroepithelium, NOT neural crest. Neural crest gives: spinal ganglia, arachnoid, adrenal medulla, sympathetic ganglia.

explanation: In the newborn infant, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris (end of spinal cord) reaches L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar punctures—needle insertion below L3 avoids spinal cord injury in adults.
keyConcept: Spinal cord in newborn reaches L3 vertebra; in adults it ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris).

explanation: Spina bifida is most common in the lumbosacral region because the lumbar and sacral vertebrae are the last to close their vertebral arches (sacral arches close last, around puberty). The most common type is spina bifida occulta at L5-S1. The thoraco-lumbar region is also a common site, but lumbosacral is the most common overall.
keyConcept: Commonest site of spina bifida = lumbosacral region; vertebrae close from cranial to caudal direction.

explanation: The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini. The nerve of the first arch is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
keyConcept: 1st arch muscles: muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor palati; nerve = CN V3.
modelAnswer: Muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (innervated by CN V3): muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.

explanation: The pharyngeal pouches give rise to important head and neck structures. The first pouch gives eustachian tube, middle ear, and mastoid air cells. The second pouch gives palatine tonsil. The third pouch gives thymus and inferior parathyroids. The fourth pouch gives superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial body. The fifth pouch gives parafollicular C cells.
keyConcept: 1st pouch= Eustachian tube/middle ear; 2nd= tonsil; 3rd= thymus/inferior parathyroids; 4th= superior parathyroids; 5th= parafollicular C cells.
modelAnswer: Derivatives of pharyngeal pouches: (1) 1st pouch: tubotympanic recess forming eustachian tube, middle ear cavity, and mastoid air cells. (2) 2nd pouch: palatine tonsil and tonsillar fossa. (3) 3rd pouch: ventral wing gives thymus; dorsal wing gives inferior parathyroid glands. (4) 4th pouch: ventral wing gives ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells); dorsal wing gives superior parathyroid glands. (5) 5th pouch: rudimentary, contributes to parafollicular C cells.

explanation: The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the skeletal elements of the face and jaw, including the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and portions of the temporal bone (squamous part). The ear ossicles malleus and incus are also first arch derivatives. Meckel's cartilage forms the malleus and incus, with endochondral ossification.
keyConcept: 1st arch skeletal: mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, malleus, incus; derived from Meckel's cartilage.
modelAnswer: Skeletal derivatives of the first branchial arch: (1) Mandible—the main bone of the lower jaw. (2) Maxilla—upper jaw. (3) Zygomatic bone—forms the cheekbone. (4) Malleus and incus—two of the three ear ossicles (stapes is 2nd arch). (5) Portions of the temporal bone (squamous part). These are derived from Meckel's cartilage, which ossifies endochondrally (except membranous bones like maxilla and zygomatic).

explanation: The upper lip forms from three prominences: the medial nasal prominences (which fuse to form the philtrum and primary palate), and the maxillary prominences (which form the lateral parts of the upper lip). Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between maxillary and medial nasal prominences. An oblique facial cleft results from failure of fusion between maxillary prominence and lateral nasal fold.
keyConcept: Upper lip: median from intermaxillary segment (medial nasal prominences); lateral from maxillary prominences. Cleft lip = failure of maxillary-medial nasal fusion.
modelAnswer: Development of the upper lip: The medial nasal prominences merge to form the intermaxillary segment, which gives the philtrum (median upper lip) and primary palate. The maxillary prominences grow medially and fuse with the medial nasal prominences to complete the upper lip. Anomalies: (1) Cleft lip—failure of fusion between maxillary prominence and medial nasal prominence on one or both sides; (2) Oblique facial cleft—failure of fusion between maxillary prominence and lateral nasal fold, running from upper lip toward the eye.

explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. All muscles, cartilages, and bones derived from the second arch are supplied by CN VII. These include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and the styloid process of the hyoid bone.
keyConcept: CN VII (facial nerve) supplies: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and styloid process.
modelAnswer: Derivatives of the second pharyngeal arch supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII): (1) Muscles—muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. (2) Bones—styloid process of hyoid bone and lesser horn of hyoid (via Reichert's cartilage). (3) Ligaments—stylohyoid ligament. All these structures are innervated by CN VII regardless of their final anatomical position.

explanation: The first pharyngeal arch is also called the mandibular arch. Its nerve is CN V3 (mandibular division of trigeminal). Skeletal derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, malleus, incus. Muscular derivatives include muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.
keyConcept: 1st arch: nerve CN V3; skeletal = mandible, maxilla, malleus, incus; muscles = mastication muscles, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani/palati.
modelAnswer: First pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, squamous temporal bone, malleus, incus (from Meckel's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini. (4) Associated structures: Meckel's cartilage (first arch cartilage), sphenomandibular ligament.

explanation: The second pharyngeal arch is also called Reichert's cartilage. Its nerve is CN VII (facial nerve). Skeletal derivatives include stapes, styloid process, lesser horn and upper body of hyoid. Muscular derivatives include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric.
keyConcept: 2nd arch: nerve CN VII; skeletal = stapes, styloid process, lesser horn/upper hyoid; muscles = facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric.
modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Facial nerve (CN VII). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Stapes, styloid process of temporal bone, lesser horn of hyoid, upper part of body of hyoid (from Reichert's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric. (4) Associated structures: Stylohyoid ligament. These muscles form the superficial muscle group of the face and some ear structures.

explanation: The third pharyngeal arch has the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) as its nerve. Skeletal derivatives include the greater horn of the hyoid and lower part of the body. The only muscular derivative is the stylopharyngeus muscle. The common carotid artery and internal carotid artery also arise from the third arch.
keyConcept: 3rd arch: nerve CN IX; skeletal = greater cornu/lower hyoid body; muscle = stylopharyngeus; vessels = common and internal carotid.
modelAnswer: Third pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Greater horn of hyoid bone and lower part of body of hyoid (from Reichert's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Stylopharyngeus muscle (the only muscle of the 3rd arch). (4) Vascular derivatives: Common carotid artery and proximal part of internal carotid artery. The stylopharyngeus is the only muscle innervated by CN IX.

explanation: The first pharyngeal arch is also called the mandibular arch. Its nerve is CN V3 (mandibular division of trigeminal). Skeletal derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, malleus, incus. Muscular derivatives include muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.
keyConcept: 1st arch: nerve CN V3; skeletal = mandible, maxilla, malleus, incus; muscles = mastication muscles, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani/palati.
modelAnswer: First pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, squamous temporal bone, malleus, incus (from Meckel's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini. (4) Associated structures: Meckel's cartilage (first arch cartilage), sphenomandibular ligament.

explanation: The second pharyngeal arch is also called Reichert's cartilage. Its nerve is CN VII (facial nerve). Skeletal derivatives include stapes, styloid process, lesser horn and upper body of hyoid. Muscular derivatives include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric.
keyConcept: 2nd arch: nerve CN VII; skeletal = stapes, styloid process, lesser horn/upper hyoid; muscles = facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric.
modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Facial nerve (CN VII). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Stapes, styloid process of temporal bone, lesser horn of hyoid, upper part of body of hyoid (from Reichert's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric. (4) Associated structures: Stylohyoid ligament.

explanation: The third pharyngeal arch has the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) as its nerve. Skeletal derivatives include the greater horn of the hyoid and lower part of the body. The only muscular derivative is the stylopharyngeus muscle. The common carotid artery and internal carotid artery also arise from the third arch.
keyConcept: 3rd arch: nerve CN IX; skeletal = greater cornu/lower hyoid body; muscle = stylopharyngeus; vessels = common and internal carotid.
modelAnswer: Third pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Greater horn of hyoid bone and lower part of body of hyoid. (3) Muscular derivatives: Stylopharyngeus muscle (the only muscle of the 3rd arch). (4) Vascular derivatives: Common carotid artery and proximal part of internal carotid artery.

explanation: The fourth pharyngeal arch is supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X). Skeletal derivatives include the thyroid cartilage, epiglottis, and cricoid cartilage (partially). Muscular derivatives include the cricothyroid muscle and the pharyngeal constrictors (except cricopharyngeus).
keyConcept: 4th arch: nerve CN X (superior laryngeal); skeletal = thyroid cartilage, epiglottis; muscles = cricothyroid, pharyngeal constrictors.
modelAnswer: Fourth pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Superior laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus, CN X). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Thyroid cartilage, epiglottis, cricoid cartilage (partially), arytenoid cartilages. (3) Muscular derivatives: Cricothyroid muscle and pharyngeal constrictors (except cricopharyngeus, which is 6th arch). The cricothyroid is the only laryngeal muscle innervated by the external laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal).

explanation: The fifth pharyngeal arch is rudimentary in humans and has no significant derivatives. Some sources consider the ultimobranchial body (which gives parafollicular C cells of the thyroid) to be a derivative of the 5th pouch. The muscles derived from the 5th arch are uncertain—some sources attribute the laryngeal intrinsic muscles to the 5th arch, but most texts assign these to the 6th arch.
keyConcept: 5th arch is rudimentary in humans; contributes to ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells of thyroid).
modelAnswer: Fifth pharyngeal arch derivatives: The 5th arch is rudimentary in humans and largely regresses. The main contribution is to the ultimobranchial body (5th pouch derivative), which gives rise to the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland that secrete calcitonin. No significant muscular or skeletal derivatives are attributed to the 5th arch. Some older classifications suggest that the oblique and transverse arytenoid muscles may be 5th arch derivatives, but the 6th arch is more commonly credited with all laryngeal intrinsic muscles.

explanation: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the tubotympanic recess, which develops into the eustachian tube, middle ear cavity, and mastoid air cells. These structures are all derived from the endoderm of the first pouch. The second pouch gives the palatine tonsil; the third pouch gives thymus and inferior parathyroids.
keyConcept: 1st pharyngeal pouch gives: eustachian tube, middle ear cavity, mastoid air cells (tubotympanic recess).
modelAnswer: Derivatives of the first pharyngeal pouch: The first pouch expands to form the tubotympanic recess, which gives rise to: (1) Pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube—connects middle ear to nasopharynx. (2) Middle ear cavity (tympanic cavity)—air-filled space containing ear ossicles. (3) Mastoid air cells—extensions of the middle ear into the mastoid process. These structures are lined by endoderm and are important clinically for spread of infection from the pharynx to the mastoid.

explanation: The second pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the palatine tonsil, which is located in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. The fossa itself is also derived from the second pouch. The second pouch also contributes to the development of the tympanic cavity and mastoid air cells (along with the first pouch).
keyConcept: 2nd pharyngeal pouch gives: palatine tonsil (and tonsillar fossa).
modelAnswer: Derivative of the second pharyngeal pouch: The palatine tonsil is the main derivative. The second pouch forms the tonsillar fossa, which houses the palatine tonsil. The tonsil is composed of lymphoid tissue and is part of Waldeyer's ring (lymphoid ring of the pharynx). The second pouch also contributes to the formation of the tympanic cavity along with the first pouch.

explanation: The third pharyngeal pouch has two derivatives: the VENTRAL wing gives the thymus gland, and the DORSAL wing gives the inferior parathyroid glands. The thymus migrates caudally with the inferior parathyroids—failure of this migration explains the variable position of inferior parathyroids and DiGeorge syndrome.
keyConcept: 3rd pharyngeal pouch: VENTRAL = thymus; DORSAL = inferior parathyroids. Both migrate caudally.
modelAnswer: Derivatives of the third pharyngeal pouch: (1) Ventral wing: Thymus gland—migrates inferiorly into the anterior mediastinum, carrying inferior parathyroids with it. (2) Dorsal wing: Inferior parathyroid glands—do not migrate as far as superior parathyroids, so have more variable positions. The third pouch also gives the parafollicular C cells (along with 5th pouch in some classifications). DiGeorge syndrome results from defective development of the 3rd and 4th pouches.

explanation: The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands (from the dorsal wing) and the ultimobranchial body (from the ventral wing, which contains neural crest cells that become parafollicular C cells of the thyroid). The superior parathyroids descend only a short distance, explaining their consistent position on the posterior aspect of the middle thyroid.
keyConcept: 4th pharyngeal pouch: DORSAL = superior parathyroids; VENTRAL = ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells).
modelAnswer: Derivatives of the fourth pharyngeal pouch: (1) Dorsal wing: Superior parathyroid glands—descend only a short distance, retaining a relatively constant position on the posterior aspect of the middle thyroid. (2) Ventral wing: Ultimobranchial body—contains neural crest-derived cells that migrate into the thyroid gland to become parafollicular (C) cells, which secrete calcitonin. The 4th pouch also contributes to the formation of the thyroid cartilage and epiglottis (along with 4th arch cartilage).

explanation: The fifth pharyngeal pouch is rudimentary in humans and contributes mainly to the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland (along with the ventral wing of the 4th pouch). Some classifications attribute the entire ultimobranchial body to the 5th pouch. It regresses without forming significant other structures. No functional parathyroids arise from the 5th pouch.
keyConcept: 5th pharyngeal pouch is rudimentary; contributes to ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells).
modelAnswer: Derivatives of the fifth pharyngeal pouch: The 5th pouch is rudimentary and largely disappears. Its main contribution is to the ultimobranchial body, which gives rise to the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland. These cells secrete calcitonin, which regulates calcium homeostasis. The 5th pouch may also contribute to the formation of the superior parathyroids (along with the 4th pouch in some classifications).

explanation: Multiple holes (fistulae) along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicate a branchial fistula, typically from the second pharyngeal cleft/cervical sinus remnant. The external auditory meatus develops from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the thymus develops from the ventral wing of the third pharyngeal pouch.
keyConcept: Multiple fistulae along sternocleidomastoid = branchial fistula (2nd cleft/cervical sinus remnant). External meatus = 1st cleft; thymus = ventral 3rd pouch.
modelAnswer: (1) Name of congenital anomaly: Branchial fistula (external branchial fistula). (2) External auditory meatus development: Develops from the deepening of the first pharyngeal cleft (ectodermal invagination between first and second branchial arches). (3) Thymus gland development: Develops from the ventral wing of the third pharyngeal pouch (endodermal).

explanation: The X-ray finding of a defect in the lower vertebral laminae with bulging meninges indicates spina bifida cystica (meningocoele). This results from failure of fusion of the dorsal portions of the vertebrae, leaving a midline defect through which meninges (and potentially spinal cord) protrude. The inability to control micturition suggests involvement of the cauda equina.
keyConcept: Defect in vertebral laminae with bulging meninges = spina bifida cystica (meningocoele); from failure of posterior neural arch fusion.
modelAnswer: (1) Condition name: Spina bifida cystica (specifically meningocoele, since meninges are bulging). (2) Embryological explanation: During the 4th week, the neural tube closes and is flanked by paraxial mesoderm that forms the vertebrae. Failure of fusion of the dorsal portions (laminae and spinous processes) of the vertebrae results in spina bifida. In spina bifida cystica, the meninges protrude through the defect forming a cyst-like swelling covered by skin or membrane. In meningocoele specifically, the meninges herniate through the defect without spinal cord involvement.

explanation: A cystic swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicates a branchial sinus (internal or external), which is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His. The superior parathyroid develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The cervical sinus is a depression between the second arch and the third, fourth, and sixth arches.
keyConcept: Cystic swelling along sternocleidomastoid = branchial sinus (cervical sinus remnant); superior parathyroids from dorsal 4th pouch.
modelAnswer: (1) Name of congenital anomaly: Branchial sinus (lateral cervical sinus). (2) Development: The branchial sinus results from failure of obliteration of the cervical sinus of His, which is a depression between the second branchial arch (operculum) and the third, fourth, and sixth arches. The cervical sinus normally disappears; if it persists, it can form a branchial cyst (no communication), sinus (single opening), or fistula (two openings). (3) Superior parathyroid development: Develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch.

explanation: The membrana tectoria is the upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament that covers the dens and cruciate ligaments of the atlas. It extends from the body of the axis to the basiocciput, covering the odontoid process. The alar ligaments connect the dens to the occipital condyles; the apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
keyConcept: Membrana tectoria = upward extension of posterior longitudinal ligament covering dens and cruciate ligaments; covers C1-C2 joint.

explanation: The alar ligaments are a pair of strong ligaments attached to the sides of the odontoid process (dens) of the axis vertebra. They connect the dens to the occipital condyles and limit rotation of the head. The apical ligament connects the tip of the dens to the anterior rim of the foramen magnum; the transverse ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas.
keyConcept: Alar ligaments attach to SIDES of odontoid process and connect to occipital condyles; limit head rotation.

explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint is a CONDYLAR (ellipsoid) joint that allows nodding (flexion and extension) and lateral bending. It does NOT allow rotation—this movement occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. The atlanto-occipital joints are synovial joints with articular capsules reinforced by anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes.
keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is CONDYLAR (ellipsoid); allows flexion/extension and lateral bending, NOT rotation.

explanation: The median atlanto-axial joint is a PIVOT (trochoid) joint that allows rotation of the head (turning the head from side to side). This is the key movement tested in the question. The lateral atlanto-axial joints are also pivot joints. The atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid and allows nodding. The apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
keyConcept: Median atlanto-axial joint is PIVOT type; allows head rotation. Atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid; allows nodding.

explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint does NOT allow rotation of the head—rotation occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. It is a condylar (ellipsoidal) synovial joint allowing flexion/extension and lateral bending. The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane is a continuation of the anterior longitudinal ligament; the posterior membrane is similar to the ligamentum flavum.
keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is synovial condylar; allows flexion/extension but NOT rotation. Anterior membrane = continuation of ALL; posterior membrane = like ligamentum flavum.

explanation: The parietal bone is a PAIRED bone—there are two parietal bones, one on each side of the skull forming the lateral walls and roof of the cranial cavity. The frontal, occipital, and sphenoid bones are unpaired (single midline bones). The ethmoid is also unpaired, forming the nasal cavity and part of the orbit.
keyConcept: Parietal bone is PAIRED (two parietal bones); forms lateral cranial wall. Frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid are unpaired.

explanation: The anterior fontanelle (soft spot) is located at the junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures and normally closes by 18-24 months of age, forming the BREMA. The pterion is the H-shaped suture junction between frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones. The lambda is the junction of sagittal and lambdoid sutures; the inion is the external occipital protuberance.
keyConcept: Anterior fontanelle ossifies to form BREMA (junction of sagittal and coronal sutures); closes by 18-24 months.

explanation: The mastoid process is a prominence on the inferior aspect of the temporal bone, posterior to the external auditory meatus. It contains air cells that communicate with the middle ear cavity. It develops after birth (visible on imaging by age 2) in response to traction from the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The squamous and petrous parts of temporal bone are also parts of the temporal bone.
keyConcept: Mastoid process is part of the TEMPORAL bone; contains mastoid air cells communicating with middle ear.

explanation: The middle cranial fossa is bounded anteriorly by the lesser wing of the sphenoid, posteriorly by the petrous temporal ridge and dorsum sellae. The floor is formed by the greater wing of the sphenoid and the squamous temporal bone. The BODY of the sphenoid (containing the sella turcica) is part of the middle cranial fossa. The crista galli and cribriform plate are part of the anterior cranial fossa; the clivus is part of the posterior cranial fossa.
keyConcept: Body of sphenoid is part of middle cranial fossa; houses pituitary gland in sella turcica.

explanation: The frontal bone is an UNPAIRED midline bone of the skull, forming the forehead, roof of the orbit, and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It articulates with the two parietal bones at the coronal suture. The nasal bone and maxillary bones are also unpaired (single midline structures); the parietal and temporal bones are paired.
keyConcept: Frontal bone is UNPAIRED; forms forehead, roof of orbit, and anterior cranial fossa floor. Parietal and temporal are paired.
